segments.say: I'm bored. Many parents hear these words many times a day. On rainy afternoons, during long car journeys, in the long weeks of summer holidays. And many parents feel a strong urge to fix it. To suggest an activity, arrange a playdate, or hand over a tablet. But some educators and researchers suggest that a little boredom might actually be good for children.

The British researcher Teresa Belton has written about the role of boredom in children's creativity. In interviews with writers and artists, she found that many described childhood boredom as a spark for imagination. Empty afternoons that turned into stories, games, inventions and worlds of their own making.

When children are constantly entertained, they may have fewer opportunities to create their own entertainment. When they're left with a little space, and a few simple materials, they often invent games, build forts, tell stories, and explore. The boredom becomes a doorway to self directed play.

Learning to cope with boredom may also be a useful life skill. If children always have boredom solved for them, they may struggle later, when life inevitably includes waiting, routine and dull tasks. Learning to sit with boredom, and to find their own ways out of it, may help them become more resourceful and independent.

Of course, this doesn't mean leaving children alone and unsupported. Children need care, attention, connection and stimulation. It's about balance. Not filling every moment for them, but trusting that, with some time and simple materials, they can often find their own way to interest and play.

Research on play has emphasized the value of unstructured, child led play, as opposed to only organized activities. The American Academy of Pediatrics, for example, has published reports highlighting the importance of free play for children's development. Free play gives children chances to make decisions, solve problems, and use their imaginations.

Simple materials often work best. Cardboard boxes, blankets, paper and pencils, blocks, sticks and stones. Toys that don't do everything by themselves leave more room for imagination. A box can be a castle, a spaceship, a cave, a car. A tablet game, however fun, usually has its own rules already built in.

And of course, this isn't only true for children. Adults, too, may benefit from unstructured time. Time without a plan, a screen or a goal. Time to wander, tinker, doodle, or simply look out of the window. Many adults have lost the habit of this kind of empty, playful time. It might be worth rediscovering.

If you're a parent, and you hear I'm bored, you might try a gentle response. Something like, that's okay, I'm sure you'll think of something. Or offer a few simple materials, and then step back. It might be uncomfortable at first, for both of you. But often, after a little while, something creative begins.

Many of us have warm memories of childhood afternoons with nothing to do. The games invented, the stories imagined, the adventures in the garden. Those empty hours were not wasted. They were where a lot of the magic happened.

So here's what we've learned about children and boredom. Childhood boredom can spark imagination and creativity. Learning to cope with boredom is a useful life skill. Free, unstructured play supports development. And simple materials, like boxes and blankets, leave room for children to invent their own worlds.

show.title: Let children be bored
items: Coping with boredom is a life skill
Simple materials leave room to imagine

segments.say: Boredom has fascinated not only psychologists, but also philosophers. Some of the greatest thinkers in history wrote about boredom as one of the deepest human experiences. Let's take a gentle walk through their ideas.
